_note: The Gym manifest (WP25a): which grammar points act as selectable form categories, grouped into picker columns. 'point' must match the grammar point title exactly (resolved to ids at request time). 'usage' is the plain-language hover explanation; 'example' is a real drill sentence from that point. 'nonstandard': entries hidden behind the 'include non-standard words' toggle.

entries.label: Subject prefixes
entries.usage: Every verb starts with a piece saying who is doing it — ni- for I, u- for you, a- for he or she — and it stays even when the pronoun is said too.
entries.example: Ninasoma kitabu. — I am reading a book.

entries.label: Present (-na-)
entries.usage: For what is happening now or what you do generally — slot -na- in after the who-prefix: ninasoma, anakula.
entries.example: Yeye anakunywa chai. — She is drinking tea.

entries.label: Present negative
entries.usage: To say you don't do something: the who-prefix goes negative, -na- disappears and the verb ends in -i — sisomi, hali.
entries.example: Mimi sili nyama. — I don't eat meat.

entries.label: Past (-li-)
entries.usage: For something that happened and finished — swap -na- for -li-: nilisoma, walikuja.
entries.example: Jana nilienda sokoni. — Yesterday I went to the market.

entries.label: Future (-ta-)
entries.usage: For anything still to come — put -ta- in the same slot: nitasoma, atakuja.
entries.example: Kesho nitaenda shule. — Tomorrow I will go to school.

entries.label: Perfect (-me-)
entries.usage: For something already done whose result still counts right now — nimekula (I've eaten), amefika (she's here).
entries.example: Nimekula chakula. — I have eaten.

entries.label: Negative past & future
entries.usage: To say it did not or will not happen — the past uses -ku- (sikusoma), the future keeps -ta- (sitasoma).
entries.example: Jana sikufanya kazi. — Yesterday I didn't do work.

entries.label: Habitual (hu-)
entries.usage: For what someone does as a rule, day in day out — hu- takes the place of both the who-prefix and the tense.
entries.example: Yeye husoma kila siku. — She reads every day.

entries.label: Narrative (-ka-)
entries.usage: When telling a story, for each next thing that happened after the first — akanunua, akarudi, instead of repeating -li-.
entries.example: Alienda sokoni, akanunua ndizi. — He went to the market and (then) bought bananas.

entries.label: Object infixes
entries.usage: To say who or what the action is done to, tuck a short piece inside the verb just before the action word itself — ninakupenda (I love you), aliniona (she saw me).
entries.example: Mimi ninakupenda. — I love you.

entries.label: Commands
entries.usage: For telling someone to do something — the bare verb to one person (Soma!), -eni to several, usi- for don't.
entries.example: Soma kitabu hiki! — Read this book!

entries.label: Subjunctive (-e)
entries.usage: After wanting, asking or telling someone to do something, the second verb drops its tense and ends in -e.
entries.example: Nataka usome kitabu hiki. — I want you to read this book.

entries.label: Was / will be
entries.usage: Because ni has no tense of its own, use kuwa to say was or will be — alikuwa mwalimu, nitakuwa daktari.
entries.example: Yeye alikuwa mwalimu zamani. — He was a teacher long ago.

entries.label: Have (nina)
entries.usage: To say you have something, Swahili says you are with it — nina kitabu, and sina pesa for haven't.
entries.example: Nina kitabu kizuri. — I have a good book.

entries.label: Compound tenses
entries.usage: For what was going on, or had already happened, at some moment in the past — two verbs: alikuwa akisoma, alikuwa amesoma.
entries.example: Nilipofika, watoto walikuwa wamelala. — When I arrived, the children had fallen asleep.

entries.label: Passive (-wa)
entries.usage: When the thing acted on matters more than whoever did it — add -w- before the last vowel: kimepikwa, kilisomwa.
entries.example: Chakula kimepikwa. — The food has been cooked.

entries.label: Causative
entries.usage: To say you make or get someone to do something — soma (read) becomes somesha (teach), rudi (go back) becomes rudisha (give back).
entries.example: Mwalimu anawasomesha watoto. — The teacher teaches the children.

entries.label: Applicative
entries.usage: To say you do it for or to someone — pika (cook) becomes pikia (cook for), andika becomes andikia (write to).
entries.example: Mama anawapikia watoto chakula. — Mother is cooking food for the children.

entries.label: Stative
entries.usage: For the state something ends up in, or what can be done, with nobody named as doing it — vunjika (be broken), someka (be readable).
entries.example: Kikombe kimevunjika. — The cup has broken / is broken.

entries.label: Reciprocal
entries.usage: When two or more people do it to each other — pendana (love each other), onana (meet), saidiana (help each other).
entries.example: Wao wanapendana sana. — They love each other very much.

entries.label: Reversive
entries.usage: To undo an action — funga (shut) becomes fungua (open), vaa (put on) becomes vua (take off).
entries.example: Tafadhali fungua mlango. — Please open the door.

entries.label: Negative infinitive
entries.usage: To say not doing something in the to-do form of the verb, where there is no who-prefix to turn negative — slot -to- in after ku-: kujua becomes kutojua.
entries.example: Alilaumiwa kwa kutosema ukweli. — He was blamed for not telling the truth.

entries.label: If / when (-ki-)
entries.usage: For an if that could really come true, with the result usually in the future — Ukisoma, utafaulu.
entries.example: Ukisoma kwa bidii, utafaulu. — If you study hard, you will succeed.

entries.label: Unless (-sipo-)
entries.usage: For if you don't or unless — the whole idea rides inside the verb: usipofanya kazi.
entries.example: Usipofanya kazi, hutalipwa. — Unless you work, you won't be paid.

entries.label: Would (-nge-)
entries.usage: For what would happen but isn't real — -nge- for now (ningesafiri), -ngali- for a past that never was (ungalifaulu).
entries.example: Ningekuwa na pesa, ningesafiri. — If I had money, I would travel.

entries.label: While -ing (-ki-)
entries.usage: For a second action going on at the same time as the main one, where English says -ing — waliondoka wakiimba.
entries.example: Waliondoka wakiimba. — They left singing.

entries.label: Impersonal verbs
entries.usage: For have to, ought to and it is possible, where nobody is the doer — the person affected goes inside the verb: inanibidi.
entries.example: Inanibidi niende hospitali leo. — I have to go to hospital today.

entries.label: Pronouns & ni
entries.usage: For saying who or what someone is — mimi, wewe, yeye with ni for am/is/are, and si for isn't.
entries.example: Mimi ni mwalimu. — I am a teacher.

entries.label: Class 1/2 (people)
entries.usage: Words for people take m- for one and wa- for many — mtoto/watoto — and the rest of the sentence copies that.
entries.example: Mtoto mmoja, watoto wawili. — One child, two children.

entries.label: Class 7/8 (things)
entries.usage: Many everyday objects take ki- for one and vi- for more than one — kitabu/vitabu, kiti/viti.
entries.example: Kitabu kimoja, vitabu viwili. — One book, two books.

entries.label: Class 5/6 (ma-)
entries.usage: A large group of nouns makes its plural with ma- — jina/majina, gari/magari — and agrees with li- and ya-.
entries.example: Jina moja, majina mengi. — One name, many names.

entries.label: Class 9/10 (n-)
entries.usage: These nouns look identical singular and plural — nyumba, simu — so the words around them tell you how many.
entries.example: Nyumba hii ni kubwa. — This house is big.

entries.label: Class 11/14 (u-)
entries.usage: For ideas like uhuru and upendo, and for long or thin things like ukuta and ufunguo; their plurals jump to the n- class.
entries.example: Uhuru ulipatikana mwaka 1961. — Independence was gained in 1961.

entries.point: Noun class Ku- (class 15: kusoma as a noun)
entries.label: Class 15 (ku-)
entries.usage: When the to-do form of a verb is used as a thing — kusoma ni muhimu, reading is important — it takes ku- agreement.
entries.example: Kuimba kwake kunanifurahisha. — Her singing pleases me.

entries.label: Place classes
entries.usage: Three ways of treating a place — pa- for an exact spot, ku- for a general or distant area, mu- for inside something.
entries.example: Mahali hapa panafaa kwa piknik. — This place is suitable for a picnic.

entries.label: Locatives (-ni)
entries.usage: To say where something is — add -ni to the noun (nyumbani, shuleni), and use kuna, pana or mna for there is.
entries.example: Watoto wako shuleni. — The children are at school.

entries.label: Adjective agreement
entries.usage: A describing word copies the prefix of the noun it describes — mtoto mzuri, watoto wazuri, kitabu kizuri.
entries.example: Watoto wazuri wanacheza. — The good children are playing.

entries.label: Possessives
entries.usage: For my, your, his and hers — the ending stays (-angu, -ako, -ake) while the front matches the noun: kitabu changu, nyumba yangu.
entries.example: Kitabu changu kiko hapa. — My book is here.

entries.label: Of (wa, ya, cha)
entries.usage: To join two nouns with of — the little linking word matches the FIRST noun: kitabu cha mtoto, nyumba ya Juma.
entries.example: Kitabu cha mtoto kiko hapa. — The child's book is here.

entries.label: This / that
entries.usage: For pointing something out — the h- words for this (huyu, hiki, hii) and the -le words for that (yule, kile, ile).
entries.example: Mtoto huyu anasoma vizuri. — This child studies well.

entries.label: Having (-enye)
entries.usage: To describe someone by what they have, where English says with — mtu mwenye pesa, nyumba yenye bustani.
entries.example: Watu wenye ulemavu wanastahili fursa sawa. — People with disabilities deserve equal opportunities.

entries.point: Numbers 11 to 100, and talking about prices
entries.label: Numbers 11–100
entries.usage: For counting past ten and asking what things cost — kumi na moja, ishirini na sita; only the small numbers change to match the noun.
entries.example: Nina miaka kumi na saba. — I am seventeen years old.

entries.point: Ordinal numbers: wa kwanza, ya pili, cha tatu
entries.label: Ordinals
entries.usage: For first, second and third — the of-word matching the noun, plus the plain number: mtu wa kwanza, siku ya pili.
entries.example: Yeye ndiye mtoto wa kwanza. — He is the first child.

entries.label: Question words
entries.usage: For asking what, who or where — nini and wapi come after the verb (Unasoma nini?), while nani can start the sentence when it names the one doing the action (Nani anakuja?).
entries.example: Unasoma nini? — What are you reading?

entries.point: Asking about time, manner and kind: lini, vipi, gani, mbona
entries.label: Lini, vipi, gani
entries.usage: For asking when (lini), how (vipi), what kind (gani, after the noun) and why on earth (mbona).
entries.example: Utarudi lini kutoka safari? — When will you return from the trip?

entries.label: Directions
entries.usage: For finding your way — X iko wapi? to ask, and kulia, kushoto, moja kwa moja to answer.
entries.example: Stesheni iko wapi? — Where is the station?

entries.label: Relative clauses
entries.usage: For who, which and that — either ambaye/ambacho after the noun, or the same marker packed inside the verb.
entries.example: Mtu ambaye anasoma ni mwalimu. — The person who is reading is a teacher.

entries.label: When-clauses (-po-)
entries.usage: For when something happened — one verb carries the whole clause: nilipofika, utakapomaliza.
entries.example: Nilipofika nyumbani, mvua ilianza. — When I arrived home, the rain began.

entries.label: How-clauses (-vyo-)
entries.usage: For as or the way that — kama unavyojua (as you know), jinsi anavyofikiri (how he thinks).
entries.example: Kama unavyojua, maisha si rahisi. — As you know, life is not easy.

entries.label: Comparing
entries.usage: For taller than, more than, as much as — the describing word never changes; kuliko, zaidi ya and kama do the work.
entries.example: Mlima Kilimanjaro ni mrefu kuliko Mlima Kenya. — Mount Kilimanjaro is taller than Mount Kenya.

entries.label: Reported speech
entries.usage: For passing on what someone said — kwamba or kuwa before the statement, and eti when you don't vouch for it.
entries.example: Alisema kwamba atarudi kesho. — He said that he will return tomorrow.

entries.label: So that (ili)
entries.usage: For saying why you are doing something — ili followed by a verb ending in -e: ninasoma ili nifaulu.
entries.example: Ninasoma kwa bidii ili nifaulu mtihani. — I study hard so that I pass the exam.

entries.label: Although
entries.usage: For although and despite — ingawa or ijapokuwa before a clause, licha ya before a noun.
entries.example: Ingawa mvua ilinyesha, tulisafiri. — Although it rained, we travelled.

entries.label: Emphasis (ndi-)
entries.usage: For singling out the one that counts — HE is the one, that is exactly when: ndiye, ndipo, ndivyo.
entries.example: Yeye ndiye aliyeiba pesa. — HE is the one who stole the money.

entries.label: Kupiga idioms
entries.usage: For dozens of everyday actions built on kupiga — kupiga simu (phone), kupiga picha (photograph), kupiga hodi (call at a door).
entries.example: Nitakupigia simu kesho asubuhi. — I will call you tomorrow morning.

entries.label: Proverbs
entries.usage: Reach for one when you want to settle a situation with a line every Swahili speaker already knows — Haraka haraka haina baraka on someone rushing.
entries.example: Haraka haraka haina baraka. — Haste, haste has no blessing.

entries.label: Respect (shikamoo)
entries.usage: When speaking to elders — greet with shikamoo, and use plural agreement for one respected person: babu wamefika.
entries.example: Mtoto alimsalimia bibi: 'Shikamoo!' — The child greeted grandmother: 'Shikamoo!'

entries.point: Greetings with habari and the possessive concord
entries.label: Greetings
entries.usage: For asking how someone is — habari yako to one person, habari yenu to several, habari za asubuhi about a time of day.
entries.example: Habari yako, Juma? — How are you, Juma?

entries.point: Introducing yourself: naitwa and jina langu
entries.label: Your name
entries.usage: For giving or asking a name — naitwa Amina or jina langu ni Amina, and unaitwa nani? to ask.
entries.example: Naitwa Fatuma Ali. — My name is Fatuma Ali.

entries.point: Telling the time: the Swahili saa system
entries.label: Telling the time
entries.usage: For clock time — Swahili counts the hours from dawn, so it runs six behind the clock face: seven in the morning is saa moja.
entries.example: Ni saa ngapi sasa? — What time is it now?

entries.point: Politeness formulas: asante, tafadhali, samahani, pole, karibu
entries.label: Courtesy words
entries.usage: The five everyday courtesies — asante (thanks), tafadhali (please), samahani (sorry), pole (sympathy), karibu (welcome).
entries.example: Asante sana kwa msaada wako. — Thank you very much for your help.

entries.point: Talking about illness: ninaumwa na and inaniuma
entries.label: Aches & pains
entries.usage: For saying what hurts — ninaumwa na kichwa (I am hurt by the head) or kichwa kinaniuma (the head hurts me).
entries.example: Ninaumwa na kichwa tangu asubuhi. — I have had a headache since morning.

entries.label: Dates & months
entries.usage: For dates and birthdays — tarehe, then the plain number, then the borrowed month name: tarehe nne Aprili.
entries.example: Nilizaliwa tarehe kumi na tatu Juni. — I was born on the thirteenth of June.

entries.point: States expressed with nina: njaa, kiu, wasiwasi, huzuni
entries.label: States with nina
entries.usage: For being hungry, thirsty, cold or worried — Swahili says you HAVE the state rather than that you ARE it: nina njaa, nina kiu, nina wasiwasi.
entries.example: Nina njaa, twende tukale. — I am hungry; let's go and eat.
